title: Labeling and Chain-of-Custody Concepts

sections.learningObjectives:
- Label specimens correctly and completely at the point of collection using two patient identifiers and required collection details, following office policy and supervision.
- Describe chain-of-custody concepts, including the purpose, documentation, secure handling, and tamper-evident integrity required for legally sensitive specimens.
- Maintain accurate, timely, legible, and permanent documentation of specimen handling and correct errors transparently per policy, without falsifying or altering records.
- Recognize specimen and documentation integrity problems and escalate them to appropriate staff following office policy and the chain of command.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A specimen label is like the name tag on your lunchbox at school; it makes sure your lunch goes to you and not to someone else, even after it gets mixed in with everyone else's bags.

### Question 2

Using two identifiers is like checking both a name and a birthday on a permission slip so you know you have the right kid, not just someone with the same first name.

### Question 3

Labeling at the patient's side is like writing your name on your test paper before you hand it in, so it never gets mixed up with anyone else's.

### Question 4

A good label is like a full address on an envelope: it has the person's full name and details so the package reaches the right home, not just 'to Sam.'

### Question 5

Put the label on the cup itself, not the lid, because lids are like hats that can be taken off and swapped by accident.

### Question 6

It is like putting the name tag on a removable hat instead of on the person; if the hats get traded, everyone has the wrong name.

### Question 7

Label the cup right away, before the person walks away, like tagging your suitcase at the airport as soon as you check it so it cannot get lost.

### Question 8

Use a permanent marker, like a laundry pen that will not wash off, so the name stays readable even if the cup gets wet.

### Question 9

Write the name on the frosted part of the glass, like writing a label on the frame of a picture instead of painting over the picture itself.

### Question 10

A specimen with no name is like a found wallet with no ID; you cannot safely give it back, so it must be thrown out and a new one is needed.

### Question 11

A room number is like a parking spot; the car parked there changes all the time, so it does not tell you who the person is.

### Question 12

If you write the wrong name on a birthday card, you cannot just scratch it out and write a new one and pretend it is fine; the safest fix is to start with a fresh card.

### Question 13

Check the label against the order like checking a receipt against what is in the bag, so the right thing goes to the right person.

### Question 14

The collection time is like the timestamp on a photo; it helps everyone understand exactly when something happened, which can change what it means.

### Question 15

Initials are like signing your name at the bottom of your homework so the teacher knows who did the work and who to ask about it.

### Question 16

If you misspell a name on a sticker, you peel it off and start fresh instead of scratching over it, so the name stays clear and readable.

### Question 17

A 24-hour collection is like a movie that must be recorded from the exact moment it starts to the exact moment it ends; you write both times on the label.

### Question 18

Saying where a sample came from is like telling someone a glass of water came from the kitchen tap and not the fish tank; it changes what the water is used for.

### Question 19

If you split a smoothie into several cups for different people, you label every cup, not just the blender, so no one drinks the wrong one.

### Question 20

If a barcode will not scan at the store, the cashier gets a fresh sticker; they do not just write the number on a scrap of paper and let the item go.

### Question 21

Label every item, like writing a name on each piece of a child's school uniform, because they can get separated in the wash.

### Question 22

Even a tiny baby gets their own name tag, just like each egg in a carton is a different egg even though they came from the same box.

### Question 23

If the name on a package label is too messy to read, the delivery person cannot know where it goes and has to send it back.

### Question 24

The safe order is like baking: check the recipe, gather the right ingredients, and write your name on the container before it goes in the shared fridge.

### Question 25

If two people at school have almost the same name, you do not guess whose lunchbox it is; you check the full name and birthday before handing it over.

### Question 26

A blood specimen travels in a sealed, spill-proof box with a warning sticker, like carrying a leaky juice bottle in a sealed bag with a 'careful' note on it.

### Question 27

A biohazard sticker is like a 'wet paint' sign; it tells people to be careful before they touch something they cannot see is risky.

### Question 28

If a juice box springs a leak, you do not grab it with bare hands and toss it in the bin; you use gloves and a spill plan so nobody gets sticky or sick.

### Question 29

Pack a specimen like you pack a fragile, secret package: sealed in a safe box with the mailing slip attached so it arrives intact and with the right instructions.

### Question 30

The requisition is like the order slip at a restaurant; it tells the kitchen exactly what was ordered and for whom, while the plate label shows which plate goes to which table.

### Question 31

Chain of custody is like a relay race sign-in sheet where every runner signs their name as they take the baton, so everyone knows exactly who carried it and when.

### Question 32

It is like sealing a package with special tape and having everyone who touches it sign a log, so no one can secretly open it and swap what is inside.

### Question 33

Some tests, like job drug tests, are like evidence in a court case; every step must be written down and signed so the answer can be trusted.

### Question 34

Routine handling is like passing a note in class; chain of custody is like every person signing the note as it is passed so the teacher can trace the whole path.

### Question 35

Every handoff is logged like signing a clipboard when you borrow the class tablet: your name, the time, and what you are doing with it.

### Question 36

A tamper-evident seal is like the sticker that tears when you open a new jar; if the seal is broken, everyone can see the jar was opened.

### Question 37

If a relay baton went missing for a few minutes and no one knows who had it, the race result would be questioned; the same is true for a specimen with a custody gap.

### Question 38

When you take the baton in a relay, you are 'on the record' the moment you grab it; you sign in right then, not after the race is over.

### Question 39

Only trained helpers get to carry the fragile trophy, and each one signs for it, because everyone must know who held it at every moment.

### Question 40

Recording the fridge temperature is like writing down the oven temperature when baking; it proves the conditions were right the whole time.

### Question 41

Keep the specimen locked up like a secret treasure, where only people with the key and permission can reach it.

### Question 42

A missing signature on the handoff log is like a blank page in a diary; you know something is missing and you tell the teacher instead of pretending it is complete.

### Question 43

Fix a mistake the way you fix a test answer: one neat line through it, write the right answer, and put your initials so everyone knows who changed it and when.

### Question 44

A witness signature is like having a second referee watch the game so there is proof that everything was done by the rules.

### Question 45

For an important test, the person shows a photo ID, like showing your student ID card before a big exam, so the results go to the right person.

### Question 46

Writing who collected the sample is like writing the name of the referee on a game report, so someone can be asked questions about it later.

### Question 47

A specimen for court is like a piece of evidence in a mystery; it must be sealed and signed for at every step so everyone knows it was not touched or switched.

### Question 48

If the safety seal on a package is broken, you do not tape it back and pretend it is fine; you tell the person in charge so the right decision is made.

### Question 49

The assistant is like a careful scorekeeper in a game; they record everything exactly by the rules and ask the referee when something is unclear, instead of making up new rules.

### Question 50

The form rides along with the specimen like a passport travels with its traveler, getting stamped at every stop along the way.

### Question 51

Write it down right away, like writing your homework in your planner the moment it is assigned, so you do not forget the details later.

### Question 52

A record is like a note in a class notebook that a substitute teacher must be able to read; clear and in pen, not scribbles or pencil.

### Question 53

Fix it like correcting a test answer: one neat line, write the right answer, and put your initials so everyone can still see what changed and who changed it.

### Question 54

A record is like a witness in court; if you erase what it said, nobody can trust the whole story anymore.

### Question 55

Full documentation is like a complete receipt: it shows who did it, when, and any special notes, so nothing important is missing.

### Question 56

An audit trail is like a breadcrumb path through the woods; you can follow it backward to see exactly how the specimen got from start to finish.

### Question 57

If a package cannot be delivered, the mail carrier leaves a note saying why; the office does the same when a specimen cannot be used.

### Question 58

If the fridge stayed too warm overnight, you write down what really happened and tell an adult, instead of pretending it was cold the whole time.

### Question 59

If someone gets hurt at work, there is a rulebook to follow and a form to fill out right away, so the person gets help and everyone learns from it.

### Question 60

A medical record is like an official scorebook; what is written in it matters later, so it has to be true and complete.

### Question 61

Type the note into the right student's file right away, like putting each test in the correct folder, and never change the date to make it look like you did it earlier.

### Question 62

If a friend asks you to change the score on a game sheet so their team wins, the right move is to say no and tell the coach, not to change it or stay quiet.

### Question 63

If the juice looks spoiled, you do not serve it and hope nobody notices; you show it to an adult and get a fresh one.

### Question 64

Before mailing a package, you check the address matches the order form, the box is the right kind, and there is enough of the item inside.

### Question 65

If a cookie fell on the floor, you do not dust it off and put it back on the plate; you throw it away and tell an adult you need a new one.

### Question 66

Integrity means the sample stays the same and keeps its name tag from the moment it is taken until the test is done, like a museum artifact that must not be changed or mislabeled.

### Question 67

A routine log is like a sign-in sheet; a chain of custody is like a relay race where every runner signs their name and time as they take the baton.

### Question 68

A patient's information is like a secret diary; you keep it closed and only let the right people look, not leave it open on the table.

### Question 69

If the name on a homework paper does not match the class list, you stop and check with the teacher instead of just filing it under a guess.

### Question 70

Handle specimens like handling raw ingredients in the kitchen: wear gloves, keep things clean, and do not get anything on the name tag.

### Question 71

Before mailing a package, you do one last check that the address, the contents, and the sealing tape are all right.

### Question 72

Some tests are like catching a bus at an exact minute; you write down the precise time you caught it, not a rough guess, because the schedule depends on it.

### Question 73

If a name tag gets smudged, you print a fresh one right away while you still know whose it is; if you are not sure, you ask an adult instead of guessing.

### Question 74

If you wrote the wrong name on a test tube of juice, you do not scratch it out and keep going; you throw it away and start a clean one with the right name.

### Question 75

Shipping a blood sample is like mailing a fragile, important item: it goes in a sealed inner container, a padded outer box, and gets the right warning stickers.

### Question 76

You cannot write 'I fed the dog' before you actually pour the food; the note must match what really happened.

### Question 77

If two classmates have similar names, you use their full names and birthdays, not just initials, to hand back the right papers.

### Question 78

Check the order like checking a recipe card before cooking: the right dish, the right amount, and any special steps, so you make exactly what was asked.

### Question 79

A requisition is like the order slip at a deli that tells the worker exactly which sandwich to make and for whom.

### Question 80

Put the sticker where it will not cover the measuring marks, like putting a name tag on the side of a measuring cup, not over the numbers.

### Question 81

If you find a cup with no name, you do not just pick a name and write it on; you tell the teacher so the right thing is done.

### Question 82

Throw away messy gloves and materials in the special bin, then wash your hands, just like throwing away a used tissue and washing up afterward.

### Question 83

If a player misses practice, the coach writes it down and tells the team; you do not pretend they showed up.

### Question 84

The chain is like a relay race where the baton is watched and signed for from the starting line all the way to the finish line, not just the first lap.

### Question 85

Hand the package over the right way: check the seal is intact, sign the handoff log yourself, and never sign someone else's name.
